subject: Post-call: Integration & quota/throttle architecture follow-up
messages:

Subject: Post-call: Integration & quota/throttle architecture follow-up

Hi Jane — great conversation earlier today. Thanks for walking us through the current search + gen flows and the volume characteristics. Quick written recap so we have alignment and clear next steps for architecture and quota decisions.

Recap / assumptions we heard from your side:
- Peak traffic: ~120 requests/s during business hours, bursts up to ~250 qps for short windows.
- Mix: ~55% embeddings (semantic search), 35% text-generation (chat & structured output), 10% reranker calls.
- Data residency: primary US, some EU traffic later this year.

Architecture recommendations (high level):
1) SDK + auth model
   - Server-side SDK integration (preferred) to avoid exposing keys in browsers.
   - API keys scoped per service (search, generation) + optional mTLS for private deployments.
   - Rotate long-lived keys via your KMS; Redwood supports key rotation hooks.

2) Routing and model variants
   - Route short-latency interactive chat to lower-latency model family; route batch embeddings to quantized models for cost efficiency.
   - Implement policy-based routing (by route name): e.g., route 'search/embeddings' to embedding pool, 'chat/structured' to low-latency pool.

3) Embeddings + reranker pattern
   - Two-phase: (A) candidate retrieval via embeddings (cheap, batched), (B) rerank with a cross-encoder or small reranker model as the second phase (can be colocated to reduce egress).
   - We recommend per-route quotas (embeddings separate from gen) and separate concurrency limits for reranking to avoid head-of-line blocking.

4) Rate limits, quotas, retries, idempotency (detailed ask from you)
   - Quotas: prefer per-api-key token-based quotas (tokens = approximate cost units). Separate buckets for embeddings vs generation.
   - Throttling behavior: soft quota first (HTTP 429 with Retry-After + x-quota-remaining headers), then hard quota cutoffs for sustained abuse.
   - Retries: clients should implement exponential backoff with full jitter. For 429s include Retry-After if present; default retry schedule: base 500ms, factor 2, max attempts 5-6.
   - Idempotency: include a client-generated Idempotency-Key for non-idempotent calls (create, fine-tune, long-running generate with monetized side-effects). For simple text generation, prefer request-scoped request_id header for tracing; treat idempotency keys as sticky for at least 24 hours.

Open/unknowns we need from your side:
- Preferred per-day and per-minute quotas for each route (embeddings, chat, reranker).
- Which calls you expect to be idempotent vs non-idempotent (e.g., billing-triggering ops).
- Any constraints on retry windows from your side (client-side SLA for how long to keep retrying).

Next steps / owners:
- Marissa (cc) to follow up with a proposed detailed diagram and suggested quota numbers by Tue EOD.
- Connor to draft SOW language for Dedicated vs Hosted throughput guarantees.
- FinCo (Jane) — confirm quota targets and whether you want us to prototype routing rules in a sandbox.

I've attached a short integration notes PDF and an auth flow diagram. Please flag anything we missed.

Thanks,
Evelyn
Evelyn Hart
Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference

Hi Jane — quick technical follow-up to answer your three points and add specifics we propose for the sandbox: 

1) Structured output / tool calling
- Yes: Redwood supports function/tool calling (schema-first). SDKs expose a function-calling primitive and validate outputs against the declared schema server-side.
- Side-effecting tools: recommend two-phase commit pattern: (A) model returns structured call intent + arguments (idempotency-key required), (B) client-side executor performs the external action and returns an execution receipt to Redwood for audit.
- Retry guidance: do not blindly retry executor-side actions. Use Idempotency-Key at the Redwood API layer to dedupe repeated model requests; executor should use the same Idempotency-Key when performing side effects.

2) Default per-route quota split (sandbox proposal)
Given your stated mix (55% embeddings, 35% gen, 10% rerank), proposed starting quotas per minute: 
- embeddings: 12k token-units/min
- generation: 8k token-units/min
- reranker: 1.5k calls/min (lower per-call cost but higher CPU)
We will provide a dashboard link for real-time counters so we can iterate.

3) 429 + rate-limit headers
Redwood will emit the following headers on throttled responses: 
- x-rw-rate-limit: overall quota units allocated
- x-rw-rate-remaining: remaining units in the current window
- x-rw-rate-reset: unix epoch (s) when the window resets
- Retry-After: seconds to wait (standard)
We also attach a short JSON body with a structured error code (e.g., RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED) and an optional mitigation hint.

4) Concrete retry + idempotency recommendations (client SDK level)
- Retry only on 429 and 5xx. Do not retry on 400-series other than 429.
- Backoff: initial 500ms, multiply by 2 on each attempt, clip at 10s, apply full jitter. Max attempts: 6.
- Idempotency: use header Idempotency-Key for any call that results in an external side-effect or creates resources. For generation calls where output billing matters, attach x-request-id for tracing; do not rely on idempotency to reconstruct streaming outputs.
- Streaming generation: if interrupted with 429, client should resume by issuing a new generation with the same conversation state and an idempotency key if deduplication is required; however, full-stream resumption is best-effort.

5) Observability hooks
We'll add x-rw-request-id in every response; you can log this and correlate in our Console for tracebacks. We can also forward per-route latency percentiles to your monitoring endpoint.

I'll drop a diagram with token-bucket thresholds and the sandbox quota numbers by EOD. If you prefer, we can spin up a short demo showing a simulated 250 qps burst and how the soft 429 window behaves.

—Marissa
